name_source: the fields in the Amoy area
source_doc: Morton H. Halperin, "The 1958 Taiwan Straits Crisis: A Documented History", RAND RM-4900-ISA (Dec 1966), unabridged/withheld pages released by Daniel Ellsberg (ellsberg.net, 2021)
quote: the U. S. military would begin by attacking a few of the fields in the Amoy area, using low-yield ten to fifteen kiloton nuclear weapons.
notes: Twining's description, under questioning by Herter at a State-JCS meeting in mid-August 1958 (the date is on printed p.75, which is not in this PDF; a cross-reference on printed p.261 points to 'the meeting on August 15'). 'A few' fields, number and names not given. Provenance study: an oral account of military planning, not a plan text. Compare printed p.264 (PDF p.104), Taylor on 2 Sep: under 'current operations plans' the 'initial attack would be on five coastal airfields with one bomb per field' with 'seven to ten Kt. air-burst weapons' (fields not named, so not a separate row).

target_class: northern limit of follow-on nuclear strikes (area)
priority: second stage (if PRC did not break off)
source_doc: Morton H. Halperin, "The 1958 Taiwan Straits Crisis: A Documented History", RAND RM-4900-ISA (Dec 1966), unabridged/withheld pages released by Daniel Ellsberg (ellsberg.net, 2021)
quote: the United States, Twining indicated, would have no alternative but to conduct nuclear strikes deep into China as far north as Shanghai.
notes: Shanghai is named as how far north the escalation would reach, not explicitly as an aim point; selected left blank. Same meeting as row 1. Twining added that this would 'almost certainly involve nuclear retaliation against Taiwan and possibly against Okinawa'.

name_source: the military control center at Ching Yang
source_doc: Morton H. Halperin, "The 1958 Taiwan Straits Crisis: A Documented History", RAND RM-4900-ISA (Dec 1966), unabridged/withheld pages released by Daniel Ellsberg (ellsberg.net, 2021)
quote: First, the Chinese Communist airfields directly opposite Taiwan and the military control center at Ching Yang should be attacked.
notes: Kuter's CINCPACAF estimate of 26 Aug 1958 (via Air Force channels), proposing nuclear use 'in increments' if aggression continued after a GRC conventional attack and a US ultimatum. The first increment also includes the unnamed 'airfields directly opposite Taiwan'. Second increment: 'selected targets within a 400-mile radius of Taiwan, including Beagle bases and control centers'. Third: 'the remainder of the targets in Annex E (the Atomic Annex) of OPS PLAN 25-58' (Halperin: 'I have not seen this Annex'). Fourth: Phase III, destruction of war-making capability. Ching Yang is not identified (Wade-Giles; possibly a place in Fujian); modern name left blank. Provenance study: a commander's proposal, not an approved plan.

name_source: the artillery pieces opposite Quemoy ... in the Amoy area
source_doc: Morton H. Halperin, "The 1958 Taiwan Straits Crisis: A Documented History", RAND RM-4900-ISA (Dec 1966), unabridged/withheld pages released by Daniel Ellsberg (ellsberg.net, 2021)
source_page: PDF p.228 (printed p.544); also PDF p.212 (printed p.528), PDF p.101 (printed p.261)
quote: whether nuclear weapons could be used to take out the artillery pieces opposite Quemoy without extensive civilian damage both in the Amoy area and on Quemoy and Taiwan.
notes: Dulles asked this after a Pentagon briefing on 7 Nov 1958. The JCS replied on 8 Dec 1958 that 'By employing air-burst weapons' the batteries could be neutralized 'with no significant radioactive fall-out implications in either the Amoy area or on Quemoy/Taiwan'. This was a feasibility answer, not a decision, so selected is blank. Earlier: on 2 Sep, Twining said it would be necessary 'to strike at Chinese Communist airfields and shore batteries with small atomic weapons' (p.261). In October, Dulles told Chiang that nuclear weapons 'could knock out the guns around Quemoy' (p.528) and that only ground bursts would be effective (p.529). Under the conventional-first decision, the same artillery and 'local airfields' were Phase II targets for conventional weapons (JCS #947298, printed p.199; Annex H Table 22, printed pp.383-384).
